correctness.rationale: For each fixed k>=2,x>=3, the complement word is established in Cloitre Proposition 4.3. Complete subtrees have discrepancy exactly 1 and every nonempty prefix is bounded between 1 and 1+h(k-1). A uniform complete-tree position, except with probability O(k^{-r}), has independent uniform child-count digits plus a bounded height-r remainder. Taking r=h^(1/3) proves an i.i.d.-CLT with mean (k-1)h/2 and variance ((k^2-1)/12)h. The stage decomposition retains fraction 1-o(1) of all positions in complete same-size W_m copies; outside offsets equal (x-k-1)log_kN+o(sqrt(log N)). Adding centers yields x-2-(k-1)/2. The exact checker successfully verified 32 complete-word/bounds cases and 27 direct-sequence/word comparisons. Finite computations do not serve as proof of the infinite limit.

evidence: Ruskey--Deugau (2009), Theorem 25, gives an exact inverse-occurrence-position formula in terms of the base-k digit sum for the associated meta-Fibonacci sequence, and Theorem 28 the first-order asymptotic U(n)~(k-1)n/k. Erickson et al. (2012), Theorem 2.1, gives first-order density constraints.
Cloitre (2026), Proposition 4.2, gives the full nested recurrence, and 4.3 the complete word.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Theorem 25 and classical base-k digit-sum probability can plausibly imply a Gaussian limit for the special x=k+1 subfamily after inversion; that special case is not advanced as separately original. The formula is for inverse occurrence positions in a more restricted meta-Fibonacci family and does not itself establish the arbitrary-x direct-index weak limit. Exact words for all x specify the data but do not state a broader distributional theorem or this stage-coupling analysis.

originality.rationale: The strongest primary antecedent supplies exact morphic words but no logarithmic Gaussian random-index fluctuation theorem. Ruskey--Deugau (2009), Theorem 25, gives a base-k digit-sum identity for inverse positions in the meta-Fibonacci special family, likely permitting the x=k+1 specialization after additional inference; it does not cover all x in the present assertion. Full primary-source comparisons and six completed semantic-index queries covered identical objects, recurrence synonyms, meta-Fibonacci sequences, tree-digit sums and Gaussian distribution synonyms; no same statement, equivalent formulation, stronger normal limit, or exact-table determination was located. A deterministic word formula in prior work does mathematically determine all statistics, but it does not itself establish the claimed nontrivial limiting distribution without the coupling and boundary argument. Unindexed earlier work remains a residual risk.
residual_risks: An unindexed source could contain a central limit theorem under a radically different terminology.

The exact word/recurrence has long been known; the x=k+1 specialization may be obtainable by standard digit-sum CLT from Ruskey--Deugau Theorem 25, so originality rests on the full arbitrary-x result and its stage boundary argument, not that isolated specialization.
The theorem is an empirical weak limit for fixed integer parameters; quantitative rates and stronger modes of convergence are unproved.

value.rationale: The first-order density U(n)/n~(k-1)/k is a natural starting point of existing tree/recurrence work. Determining the typical residual, including its logarithmic drift and nondegenerate Gaussian scale, is a genuine second-order quantitative question. The result covers all fixed k>=2,x>=3, extends the older special k-ary tree family, and gives universal variance coefficient (k^2-1)/12 with initial-condition-dependent drift. It motivates refinements of nested-recurrence asymptotics and is not a textbook restatement of the exact-word identity.
